practiceSet.title: U3.LT2 Practice: Ionic Bonds and Naming
practiceSet.description: Practice explaining how ionic bonds form (electron transfer and ions), writing ionic formulas, and naming ionic compounds with polyatomic ions and Roman numerals.

activity.title: U3.LT2 Relearning: Ionic Bonds and Naming
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can explain how ionic bonds form and name ionic compounds.

**Think of lunch money.** If a friend hands you a dollar, the dollar moves from them to you: one gives and one takes. An **ionic bond** works the same way. A **metal** atom (the giver) **transfers** its valence electrons to a **nonmetal** atom (the taker).

**How the bond forms.** 1) The metal **loses** its valence electrons and becomes a **positive ion**. 2) The nonmetal **gains** those electrons and becomes a **negative ion**. 3) **Opposite charges attract**, and that attraction is the ionic bond. Both atoms end up with a full outer level, which makes them stable. Only electrons move; the protons never change.

**Charges from the group number:** Group 1 = +1, Group 2 = +2, Group 13 = +3, Group 15 = −3, Group 16 = −2, Group 17 = −1.

**The charges must cancel to zero.** Think of paying with exact change. Sodium gives 1 electron and chlorine takes 1, so one of each works: NaCl. Magnesium gives 2, but each chlorine takes only 1, so it takes two chlorines: MgCl₂. **Criss-cross** is the shortcut: each charge drops to the bottom as the subscript on the other ion, then **reduce** and **check** that the charges add to zero. The metal always goes first.

**Naming ionic compounds.** Metal first, then the nonmetal with an **-ide** ending (chlorine → chloride, oxygen → oxide). **No prefixes, ever.** A **polyatomic ion keeps its own name** (sodium nitrate), and it gets parentheses in a formula only when you need 2 or more of it (Ca(NO₃)₂). Metals with more than one charge (transition metals like Fe and Cu, plus Pb and Sn) need a **Roman numeral**, which is the **charge**, not the number of atoms. Group 1, 2 and 13 metals never get one.

**Worked example 1:** How do calcium and fluorine bond? Calcium (Group 2) has 2 valence electrons to give. Each fluorine (Group 17) takes 1. So calcium gives one electron to each of two fluorines: Ca²⁺ and two F⁻ make CaF₂, **calcium fluoride**.

**Worked example 2:** Name Fe₂O₃. Iron needs a numeral. Three oxides are 3 × (−2) = −6, so two irons total +6, and each iron is +3. Answer: **iron(III) oxide**.

**Worked example 3:** Write the formula for magnesium nitrate (nitrate is NO₃⁻). Mg²⁺ and NO₃⁻: criss-cross gives 1 magnesium and 2 nitrates. Answer: **Mg(NO₃)₂**.

**Watch out for:** saying the atoms share electrons (that is covalent), saying the metal gains electrons, changing the number of protons, prefixes on ionic names ("calcium dichloride"), using a subscript as the Roman numeral (Fe₂O₃ is not iron(II)), and putting -ide on a polyatomic ion.
prompts: Explain how sodium and chlorine form an ionic bond. Say what each atom's valence electrons do and what ions form.
Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂, not MgCl. Explain why it takes two chlorine atoms for every magnesium atom.
Name these compounds and explain your thinking for each: K₂S, CuCl₂ (chloride is Cl⁻), and Na₂SO₄ (sulfate is SO₄²⁻).
Write the formula for aluminum oxide. Show how the charges cancel to zero.
